children: Japan is expanding 5G and digital infrastructure cooperation in India through local manufacturing, photonic networks, data centres and submarine cables

Japan is expanding its digital infrastructure footprint in India through local 5G software development and equipment manufacturing, while Japanese companies are also working with Indian partners on all-photonic networks, data centres and submarine cables, Hideo Fuseda, Vice-Minister for Policy Coordination (International Affairs), Japan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications.

Rakuten Symphony is developing 5G software solutions in India with Tejas Networks, while NEC is working with the Indian telecom equipment maker to localise production of 5G radio units. Olexai is also working with Indian partners on local manufacturing of 5G radio units for Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited’s (BSNL) network deployment, Fuseda said.

“Japanese companies are not simply bringing Japanese technology to India. They are developing software, manufacturing equipment and building local capability here in India,” Fuseda said while speaking at said at India Mobile Congress 2026.

The projects represent Japan’s contribution to India’s push to develop domestic digital infrastructure, with the focus extending beyond supplying telecom technology to establishing capabilities within the country. Fuseda said the approach was also linked to Japan’s wider cooperation with India on infrastructure required for the expansion of artificial intelligence.
“This is our contribution to make in India and to India's digital infrastructure for the AI era,” he said.

The cooperation extends beyond 5G equipment. Onefinity, a Fujitsu Group company, has established a local subsidiary in India to strengthen support for all-photonic networks and is planning to launch an APN laboratory named ONIC India, according to Fuseda.

NTT and Japan International Cooperation and Investment Company (JICT) are supporting data-centre deployment and operations in Mumbai, while also developing submarine cable connectivity between Singapore and India. Fuseda said the projects would strengthen high-capacity international connectivity as digital traffic and computing requirements increase.
AI Drives Demand For Digital Infrastructure

The initiatives come under Japan’s HOIP Digital Corridor Initiative, which seeks to develop a trusted and resilient digital ecosystem across the Indo-Pacific. The initiative covers submarine cables, mobile networks, data centres and cloud, all-photonic networks and non-terrestrial networks, linking infrastructure across land, sea, air and space.

Fuseda said the infrastructure requirement was changing as artificial intelligence moves into industrial and consumer applications, increasing demand for computing resources and networks capable of connecting those resources. He said AI would increasingly operate across factories, hospitals, vehicles, cities and logistics rather than remain confined to conventional data centres.
“As AI becomes part of our daily lives and industry, we will need more data centres and cloud capacity to support AI services,” Fuseda said.

The expansion of computing infrastructure will also require networks capable of linking data centres and users at different points of the network, according to Fuseda. He said AI applications would increasingly operate at the network edge, requiring connectivity that can move data between computing resources and end users with greater speed and reliability.
“We need advanced networks and connected data centres for AI and users, quickly, reliably, and everywhere,” he said.

Energy consumption is another consideration in Japan’s approach to next-generation digital infrastructure. Fuseda said the growth of AI and data centres would increase electricity requirements, making it necessary to expand computing and network capacity without allowing energy consumption to rise at the same rate.

Japan is consequently placing all-photonic networks, or APN, at the centre of its future network strategy. Fuseda said the technology could support high-speed connectivity while improving energy efficiency, making it relevant to the infrastructure requirements created by the expansion of AI.
“This is why we place all photonic networks, which we call APN, at the heart of our future network,” Fuseda said.
Explore AI And Mobility Applications

Japanese companies are also working with Indian firms on applications that use connectivity and AI beyond conventional telecom services. ATARink is working with Indian company Softdel Systems on wireless power technology combined with AI and cloud solutions for physical AI, while Honda is using connected-vehicle data for road-condition management and smart mobility.

ZeroSun is working with Indian partners on vehicle-to-everything (V2X) technologies and intelligent transportation systems, Fuseda said. These projects, he added, illustrate how digital infrastructure can support applications in mobility and other sectors rather than being limited to connectivity.
“The real goal is to use AI and digital technology to create value for people, businesses, and society,” Fuseda said.

Fuseda said Japan and India could combine their respective capabilities as digital infrastructure requirements expand. India’s scale, talent and digital ecosystem, he said, could complement Japanese technology and experience in developing infrastructure for the AI era.
“Japan and India have complementary strengths by combining India's scale, talent, and dynamic digital ecosystem with Japan's technology and experience,” Fuseda said.
He said cooperation between the two countries could support the development of infrastructure needed for AI while creating applications intended to deliver economic and social benefits.
